aligned_passages.text:
The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

### 9.1 Smoothness of the minimizing coefficient Full support does not by itself prove that the Stieltjes measure has a density. In the source manuscript, that conclusion uses the PDE again after the gap contradiction has established $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$. We reconstruct the additional argument here because it explains a further conclusion of the original paper. It is not a clause of the selected full-support formal statement. Put $f_k=\partial_x^k\Phi_\gamma$, so $f_1=u$ and $f_2=a$. All formulas in this subsection are on a fixed compact time strip, where every finite collection of spatial derivatives is bounded. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula along the associated diffusion gives $$ df_k(t,X_t)= -\frac{\gamma(t)}2\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j} f_{j+1}(t,X_t)f_{k-j+1}(t,X_t)\,dt +f_{k+1}(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ The sum is empty when $k=1$. This identity needs no derivative of $\gamma$. For an initially nonsmooth coefficient, apply it to finite-step approximations and pass to the integrated identity: the coefficient converges in $L^1$, the spatial factors converge uniformly, and the stochastic integrals converge by the Itô isometry. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, smooth-density proof, lines 35–50][fs-density]. Set $b=f_3$. The case $k=2$ gives $da=-\gamma a^2dt+b\,dB_t$, and consequently $$ 0=\frac d{dt}\mathbb E a^2 =\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma(t)\mathbb E a^3 \quad\text{for almost every }t<1. $$ Convexity gives $a\geq0$; the already established second moment gives $\mathbb E a^3\geq(\mathbb E a^2)^{3/2}=1$. Thus the quotient $$ \widetilde\gamma(t)=\frac{\mathbb E b(t,X_t)^2} {2\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^3} $$ is well defined and continuous, before any continuity of $\gamma$ is known. It equals $\gamma$ almost everywhere. Approaching an arbitrary $t<1$ from the right through the full-measure equality set, continuity of $\widetilde\gamma$ and right continuity of $\gamma$ give equality at that $t$ as well. This proves continuity of $\gamma$. At zero, $X_0=0$, and evenness of $\Phi(0,\cdot)$ gives $b(0,0)=0$; hence $\gamma(0)=0$. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, lines 52–66][fs-density]; [Chen, Proposition 4.6, pp. 25–26][chen26]. The bootstrap must treat all polynomial moments simultaneously. For a polynomial $P$ in finitely many variables, write $$ M_P(t)=\mathbb E P(f_1(t,X_t),\ldots,f_m(t,X_t)). $$ The preceding stochastic identities and Itô's product rule provide polynomials $Q_P,R_P$, involving only finitely many additional derivatives, such that $$ M_P(t)-M_P(0)=\int_0^t\bigl(M_{Q_P}(s)+\gamma(s)M_{R_P}(s)\bigr)\,ds. $$ Explicitly, if $$ D_k(y)=-\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j}y_{j+1}y_{k-j+1}, $$ then $$ Q_P=\tfrac12\sum_{k,l}\partial_{kl}P\,y_{k+1}y_{l+1}, \qquad R_P=\sum_k\partial_kP\,D_k. $$ All these moments start continuous. Once $\gamma$ is continuous, the integral formula makes every moment $C^1$, and the quotient formula makes $\gamma$ itself $C^1$. If all moments and $\gamma$ are $C^r$, the same argument makes them $C^{r+1}$. Induction proves $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Since $\gamma(0)=0$, there is no atom at zero; its Stieltjes measure is $\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and monotonicity gives $\gamma'\geq0$. This is the polynomial-moment method credited by the source to Auffinger–Chen and to Chen's zero-temperature treatment. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, lines 68–101][fs-density]; [Auffinger and Chen, proof of Theorem 2(ii), p. 16][ac-properties]; [Chen, Appendix B.6, p. 38][chen26]. The exact arXiv edition of Auffinger–Chen's polynomial-moment proof has a local display discrepancy: p. 16 of arXiv:1303.3573v1 prints a square in $F_3$ below (40), whereas Proposition 3, p. 9, has the cube. The identity $d(a^2)=(-2\gamma a^3+b^2)dt+2ab\,dB$ requires the cube used above; the moment induction itself is unchanged.

### 9.2 Why the density is strictly positive away from zero This is a further consequence of full support, not an input to it or to §6. A smooth increasing function can have zero derivative at an interior point. For example, $g(t)=(t-\tfrac12)^3+\tfrac18$ on $[0,1)$ is nonnegative and strictly increasing, and $dg$ has full support, although $g'(\tfrac12)=0$. This example is not a minimizing coefficient; it disproves only the inference from strict increase to a positive derivative. The minimizing density needs a further estimate. The smoothness just proved permits (4.2), now with $q(t)=t$. Writing $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, it becomes $$ 2\gamma'(t)\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma(t). $$ Fix $t\in(0,1)$ and set $c=\gamma(t)>0$, using full support and $\gamma(0)=0$. The coefficient is now smooth, so Proposition 4.1 applies at this time to the same diffusion. Its proof uses nonminimizing local constant replacements, with compact-strip bounds independent of the widths of the inserted plateaus. **Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. A separate boundary estimate excludes terminal
gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and smoothness; a local
constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We explain the construction and uses of
the quantitative estimate while importing its shape comparisons and
full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value identity and
state the classical optimisation consequence and the additional steps
leading to asymptotically optimal quantum approximate optimization
algorithm (QAOA) circuits.

[Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1][ACZ] proved infinite support. This need not be full support: the measure $\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-k}\delta_{1-2^{-k}}$ has infinitely many atoms and many gaps. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][Chen] subsequently proved full support and smooth nonnegative density. We follow OpenAI's quantitative proof of the support conclusion and its further strict-positivity result. The feature used twice is a lower bound valid throughout every positive constant interval of an admissible coefficient, without a minimising assumption. **Theorem 1 (full support; [OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][FS]).** If $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimises $\mathcal P$, then $$ \operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1),\qquad \gamma(t_2)>\gamma(t_1)\quad(0\leq t_10$. This second use needs the estimate for a local constant replacement that need not minimise, without requiring $q''=0$ at the comparison time. Its explicit positive margin must also survive the replacement's limit. Section 5 derives the scalar value formula and identifies the finite Gaussian observable used by the separate QAOA theorem. These optimisation consequences use full support; strict density positivity is a further analytic conclusion. We assume Itô calculus and martingale convergence. Omitted proofs are linked to *From Parisi full support to deterministic QAOA circuits: A long reasoning record*, the [companion edition of 26 October 2026](../long/reasoning-record.md); original-source citations remain beside the imported inputs.

Full support does not force pointwise positive density. For instance, $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t(s-\tfrac12)^2\,ds$ has full Stieltjes support but $\gamma'(\tfrac12)=0$: every interval of positive length has a positive integral, although the integrand vanishes at one point. The quantitative remainder in (5) rules this out for a minimiser. First, the identity $\mathbb E a^2=1$ expresses $\gamma$ as a quotient of continuous moments and then gives smoothness. Only afterwards do we apply the fixed-time spatial estimate to obtain $\gamma'>0$. **Corollary 4 (smooth positive density; [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 6.4][FS]).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Its Stieltjes measure is $\mu_\gamma(dt)=\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and $$ 2\gamma'(t)\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^3] \geq\frac{\gamma(t)^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \qquad(0[long §9.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence). Now the two differentiated moments are $$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E b^2=\mathbb E[d^2-6\gamma ab^2], \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E a^3=\mathbb E[3ab^2-3\gamma a^4]. $$ For a smooth time coefficient, differentiating $q''=\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma\mathbb E a^3$ therefore gives $$ q^{(3)}+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3 =\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \tag{9} $$ This identity displays the two uses of the same spatial moment. On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$ and $(v,w,z)=c(a,b,d)$ recover (4). For the now smooth minimiser, $q=t$, so $q^{(3)}=0$ and the left side is $2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3$. Proposition 3 supplies the lower bound for this spatial moment. Apply Proposition 3 to the now smooth minimiser. In particular, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \mathbb E a^3\leq\sqrt{\mathbb E a^2\,\mathbb E a^4} =\sqrt{\mathbb E a^4}\leq\mathbb E a^4, $$ so the same inequality implies $\gamma'(t)\geq\gamma(t)^2/2000$ for $0[Long §§9.1–9.2](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence) retain the smoothness argument and fixed-time transfer, including the common approximation bounds. **Relation to earlier estimates.** The backward shape comparisons, transformed density and positive-temperature gap-crossing argument appear in [Lopatto (2026), v3, Propositions 3.6, 7.1 and 9.1][Lopatto]. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Proposition 4.2][Chen] proves the zero-temperature crossing implication $q''=0\Rightarrow q'''>0$ under the minimiser convention of §3.1. The quantitative bound (3) holds throughout a positive plateau of any admissible coefficient. Arbitrary-coefficient scope alone does not distinguish it from the later literature: [Lopatto's v4, Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.6][Lopatto-v4] give qualitative crossing for arbitrary positive-temperature probability measures. [Lopatto's external-field paper, Theorem 2.3, §8 and Appendix B][Lopatto-field] also uses a fixed-time spatial inequality for both support and density, with different terminal data, one-sided coefficient bounds and scalar hypotheses. The distinction relevant here is the fourth-moment margin available without a stationarity condition at the comparison time. The precise edition and hypothesis comparisons are in [long §2.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#prior-work-comparison).

Full support alone does not give a density. Additional differentiation of the identities $q=t$ and $\mathbb E[a^2]=1$, followed by another use of the integrated curvature estimate on locally constant comparison coefficients, proves that $\gamma$ is smooth, $\gamma(0)=0$, and $\mu_\gamma=\gamma'(t)\,dt$ with $\gamma'(t)>0$ for $0[§§9.1–9.2](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence), supplies this additional argument; Chen's earlier theorem had already given smooth nonnegative density and full support.
